abstract.p: The present invention is related to novel ginger-based compositions for the treatment of atherosclerosis and related conditions. Standardized ginger extracts included as components of the proprietary composition, "ROZ20", were tested in-vivo for their effect on reducing atherogenic modifications of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and on reducing or substantially preventing the development of atherosclerosis. The study was performed in apolipoprotein E deficient (Eo) mice. At the end of 10 weeks of consumption of 250 microgram/day, "ROZ20", the entire aorta of the mice were examined for atherosclerotic lesions. The mean lesion area of the ROZ20-treated mice was reduced by 67 % in comparison to the lesion area of placebo-treated mice. These results clearly demonstrate that administration of "ROZ20" for a period of 10 weeks to the atherosclerotic Eo mice has a significant beneficial effect in substantially reducing the size and rate of development of atherosclerotic lesions.

La présente invention concerne de nouvelles compositions à base de gingembre destinées à traiter l'athérosclérose et les états apparentés. Cette composition renferme notamment, comme composants, des extraits de gingembre normalisés, ci-après dénommés "ROZ20", analysés in vivo afin de déterminer s'ils peuvent réduire les modifications athérogènes de la lipoprotéine de basse densité (LDL), et faire diminuer ou au moins sensiblement prévenir la progression de l'athérosclérose, cette étude ayant été conduite chez une souris carencée en alipoprotéine E (Eo). Après 10 semaines au cours desquelles cette souris a consommé 250 microgrammes par jour de ROZ20, la totalité de l'aorte de cette souris a été examinée afin de détecter toute lésion athéroscléreuse. On a ainsi découvert que la région moyenne des lésions de ladite souris traitée avec ROZ20 a diminué de 67 % par rapport à la région des lésions d'une souris traitée au placebo. Ces résultats montrent donc clairement que l'administration de ROZ20 à une souris Eo atteinte d'athérosclérose sur une période de 10 jours a un effet bénéfique considérable et permet de réduire sensiblement la taille et la progression des lésions athéroscléreuses.

description.p: NOVEL COMPOSITIONS FOR THE TREATMENT OF ATHEROSCLEROSIS AND RELATED CONDITIONS
FIELD AND BACKGROUND
The present invention is related to novel compositions for the treatment
of atherosclerosis and related conditions, and in particular, is related to novel
compositions which include 6-shogaol, 6-gingerol or a mixture thereof, or one
or more of 8-gingerol, 10-gingerol, 8-shogaol or 10-shogaol, dried ginger
rhizome, or a novel combination of an extract and dried ginger rhizome, as well
as methods for the use of these novel compositions.
Atherosclerosis is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in the
western world and its pathogenesis involves complicated interactions between
cells of the arterial wall, blood cells, and plasma lipoproteins (1). The early
atherosclerotic lesion is characterized by foam cells, which are derived from
cholesterol loaded macrophages (2,3). Macrophage cholesterol accumulation
and foam cell formation are the hallmark of early atherogenesis and most of the
cholesterol in these cells is derived from plasma low-density lipoprotein (LDL).
Native LDL however, has to undergo some modifications in order to cause
extensive macrophage cholesterol accumulation (4-6).
Two major modifications with potential pathological significance are
LDLoxidation (7,8) and lipoprotein aggregation (9, 10). Both of these
modifications lead to increased macrophage uptake of the modified lipoprotein,
followed by cellular cholesterol accumulation and foam cell formation (7-10).

Both oxidized LDL (Ox-LDL) and aggregated LDL (Agg-LDL) were shown to
be present in the atherosclerotic lesion of humans and of the apolipoprotein - E
deficient (E ) mice ( 1 1 , 12). While the increased uptake of Ox-LDL is mediated
via scavenger receptor(s), which are not regulated by the cellular cholesterol
content (4. 13), the enhanced uptake of aggregated LDL involves phagocytosis,
which is mediated via the LDL receptor (9, 10) The involvement of Ox-LDL
in atherosclerosis is suggested from its presence in the atherosclerotic lesion,
from the increased susceptibility to oxidation of LDL derived from
atherosclerotic patients, such as hypercholesterolermic, as well as from the
atherosclerotic apolipoprotein E-deficient (E ) mice, and also from the anti-
atherogenicity of several dietary antioxidants (8). The involvement of LDL
aggregation in atherosclerosis is also suggested from the presence of such
modified LDL in human atherosclerotic lesion, as well as in the aortas from E
mice (12).
Oxidative modification of LDL in the arterial wall can also lead to
acceleration of the atherosclerotic process, secondary to macrophage foam cell
formation. Macrophage foam cell formation involves the transport of both LDL
and monocytes into the arterial wall. Monocytes can adhere to the endotheluim
under certain pathological conditions, followed by migration into the arterial
wall and differentiation to macrophages (Figure 1). Plasma LDL can also be
transported into the arterial wall, where arterial wall cells and matrix
components can lead to its oxidation and aggregation (Figure 1).
Oxidative modification of LDL in the arterial wall during early

atherogenesis is probably mediated mainly by the action of monocyte-derived
macrophages. Arterial wall macrophages were shown to accumulate oxidized
lipids in areas of the atherosclerotic lesion and these cells can oxidize LDL m
the vascular interstitial space. Activation of the cellular oxygenases can result
in the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can induce the oxidation
of extracellular LDL. LDL oxidation by macrophages depends on the oxidative
status of the macrophages (the balance between cellular oxygenases and
cellular antioxidants), as well as by the LDL oxidative status (the balance
between the LDL substrates which are prone to oxidation and LDL-associated
antioxidants).
In the arterial wall, macrophage oxygenases such as NADPH oxidase
and lipoxygenase (14-16), and cellular antioxidants such as the glutathione
system, including reduced glutathione (GSH) and the enzymes gluthatione
peroxidase, reductase and transferase (8), determine the capacity of the cells to
oxidatively modify LDL. In addition to the cellular oxidative status, LDL
polyunsaturated fatty acids and cholesterol content, and the antioxidants in the
LDL environment (intrinsic constituents such as vitamin E, β-carotene,
lycopene and polyphenolic flavonoids, and extrinsic components such as
vitamin C) also affect LDL oxidation. Vitamin E is the most abundant
antioxidant in LDL, and dietary supplementation of vitamin E was shown to
increase the resistance of LDL to oxidation (17, 18). The carotenoids β-
carotene and lycopene possess some oxidative capabilities, though to a limited
extent and probably only in unique oxidative systems, such as those producing

singlet oxygen radicals (19-23).
In addition, the phenolic flavonoids are also anti-oxidants which appear
to be able to prevent certain of the pathogenic processes associated with
atherosclerosis. The polyphenolic flavonoids constitute a large class of related
compounds consisting of two phenylbenzene (chromanol) rings linked through
a pyran ring. Consumption of phenolic flavonoids in the diet was shown to be
inversely associated with morbidity and mortality from coronary heart disease
(24-27). Different classes of flavonoids are present in different fruits,
vegetables, and beverages such as tea and wine. Flavonoids may prevent
coronary artery disease by reducing platelet aggregation, by reducing damage
from ischemia and reperfusion, or by inhibiting LDL oxidation. The
antioxidant activity of the flavonoids is related to their chemical structure
(28,29). Polyphenol constituents in olive oil were shown to contribute to the
inhibition of LDL oxidation (30, 31). Consumption of black or green tea,
which are rich in another subclass of polyphenols, was shown to be associated
with an increase in plasma antioxidant potential (32).
The "French paradox", i.e. the low incidence of cardiovascular events in
the general French population despite the high level of saturated fat in the diet,
was attributed to regular drinking of red wine, a dietary source of polvphenols.
Ingestion of red wine was shown to be associated with increased antioxidant
activity in serum (33, 34). Frankel et al. reported (35) that flavonoids extracted
from Califonian red wine protected LDL against oxidation when added in vitro.
Furthermore, the long-term consumption of red wine was shown to inhibit LDL

oxidation ex vivo (36). The inventors of the present Application have recently
demonstrated that consumption of red wine rich in catechin (flavanol) and
quercetin (flavonol) with meals results in reduced susceptibility of LDL to
oxidation (37), and in reduced progression of atherosclerosis in the atherogenic
apolipoprotein E deficient mice (38). Crude extract of licorice, derived from the
rhizomes of the Asian plant Glycyrrhiza glabra, which is also a nutrient rich in
polyphenols (mainly glabridin), was recently shown to protect LDL against
lipid peroxidation in vitro and in vivo in normal healthy human volunteers (39).
Ginger (Zingiber Officinale Roscoe) is one of the world best known
spices, and has also been universally used throughout history for its health
benefits. The dried extract of ginger includes many different substances, such
as essential oils containing monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes. As shown in
Figure 2A, the gingerols and shogaols, and related phenolic ketone derivatives,
can also be found in ginger. Ginger extract was shown to possess antioxidative
characteristics, and can significantly scavenge superoxide anion and hydroxyl
radical (40). Gingerols isolated from Z. officinale was shown to inhibit platelet
function due to inhibition of thromboxane formation (41), and the compounds
found in ginger also appeared to interfere with the process of inflammation
(42). High concentrations of gingerols inhibited ascorbate/Fe -induced lipid
peroxidation in rat liver microsomes (43).
Furthermore, feeding ginger to rats significantly elevated the activity of
hepatic cholesterol-7-alpha-hydroxylase, the rate limiting enzyme of bile and
biosynthesis. This elevated activity stimulated the conversion of cholesterol to

bile acids, and thus the elimination of cholesterol from the body (44).
Furthermore, a pure constituent from ginger (E-8 beta, -17 epoxylabd- 12-ene-
15, 16-dial (ZT)) was shown to inhibit cholesterol biosynthesis in homogenated
rat liver (45).
However, none of the components of ginger has been shown to alter or
prevent the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in an experimental animal model.
Even whole ginger has not been shown to have any such effects on the process
of atherosclerosis. Since ginger has been consumed as a spice for thousands of
years, if any of the components of ginger were shown to have such favorable
anti-atherosclerotic activity, the relative safety of such components would be
quite likely. Thus, determining if any component or components of ginger is
able to exert such effects would be very useful for the treatment and prevention
of coronary disease.
There is thus a need for, and it would be useful to have, a composition
for the treatment or prevention of atherosclerosis and related conditions, such as
coronary disease, strokes and cardiac arrest, which would be derived from a
foodstuff such as ginger, and which would include one or more components of
ginger or even whole dried ginger.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
According to the present invention there is provided a composition for
treating an atherosclerotic condition, comprising a component selected from the
group consisting of 6-shogaol, 8-shogaol, 10-shogaol, 6-gingerol, 8-gingerol

and 10-gingerol, and a mixture thereof. Preferably, the component is selected
from the group consisting of 6-shogaol and 6-gingerol. More preferably, the
component is 6-shogaol. Alternatively and preferably, the component is 6-
gingerol.
According to another embodiment of the present invention there is
provided a method for the treatment of an atherosclerotic condition in a subject,
comprising the step of administering a pharmaceutically effective amount of a
component selected from the group consisting of a 6-shogaol, 8-shogaol, 10-
shogaol, 6-gingerol, 8-gingerol and 10-gingerol, and a mixture thereof; dried
ginger rhizome alone or in combination with one of the aforementioned
ingredients; and ROZ20, alone or in combination with one of the aforementioned
ingredients.
Preferably, the component includes ROZ20. More preferably, the
component is selected from the group consisting of a 6-shogaol, 8-shogaol, 10-
shogaol, 6-gingerol, 8-gingerol and 10-gingerol, and a mixture thereof. Also
preferably, the component includes dried ginger rhizome.
According to yet another embodiment of the present invention, there is
provided a method for preparation of a ginger extract, the method comprising the
steps of: (a) extracting ginger rhizome with a first volume of an ethanol solvent to
form a first extract and a first residue; (b) separating the first extract and the first
residue; (c) evaporating the first extract to form a dried extract; and (d) mixing
the dried extract with dried, powdered ginger rhizome to form the standardized

ginger extract.
Preferably, the step of mixing the dried extract with the dried, powdered
ginger rhizome is performed by microencapsulating the dried extract and the
dried, powdered ginger rhizome. Also preferably, the ethanol solvent is 90%
(VW) ethanol.
Preferably, the method further comprises the steps of: (e) extracting the
first residue with a second volume of the ethanol solvent to form a second extract
and a second residue; (f) separating the second extract and the second residue; (g)
extracting the second residue with a third volume of the ethanol to form a third
extract and a third residue; (h) separating the third extract and the third residue;
(i) combining the first extract, the second extract and the third extract to form a
combined extract; (j) evaporating the combined extract to form a combined dried
extract; and (k) mixing the combined dried extract with the dried, powdered
ginger rhizome to form the ginger powder extract.
Preferably, the ginger rhizome is milled ginger rhizome.
According to still another embodiment of the present invention, there is
provided a composition for the treatment of atherosclerosis, comprising a
composition prepared according to any of the above methods.
Hereinafter, the term "ginger" refers to any part of the plant Zingiber
Officinale Roscoe. Hereinafter, the term "whole dried ginger" refers to any
portion of the ginger rhizome itself which has been dried to remove at least a
portion of the moisture present in the rhizome when harvested, but specifically
excludes extracts of the ginger rhizome. Hereinafter, the term "component of
ginger" refers to a molecule selected from the group consisting of 6-shogaol, 8-

DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS
The present invention is related to novel compositions for the treatment
of atherosclerosis and related conditions, and methods for their use thereof.
The compositions of the present invention include the ROZ20 composition of
the present invention, as well as 6-shogaol, 6-gingerol or a mixture thereof, or
one or more other components of ginger, or whole dried gmger rhizome, or
mixtures of whole dried ginger rhizome and one or more components of ginger
thereof.
As described in further detail in the Examples below, a standardized
ginger extract included as a component of the ROZ20 composition of the
present invention was first analyzed to determine the identity of the
components of the extract. The results of this analysis are shown in Example 1.
These results demonstrate that the main components of the ginger extract, and
hence of the ROZ20 composition of the present invention, are 6-shogaol and 6-
gingerol, which are the particularly preferred components of ginger in the
composition of the present invention.
Next, ROZ20 was tested in vivo for its effect on reducing atherogenic

modifications of LDL and on reducing or substantially preventing the
development of atherosclerosis. The atherogenic modifications examined
included oxidation and aggregation of LDL. The study was performed in
apolipoprotein E deficient (E ) mice. These mice have a "knockout" for the
apolipoprotein E gene, and are used as an animal model for atherosclerosis. The
mice develop atherosclerosis through a pathogenic process which is highly
similar to the equivalent process in humans. This pathogenic process is
substantially accelerated by a high cholesterol diet, and the resultant
atherosclerotic plaque resembles the atherosclerotic lesions found in humans.
Example 1
Preparation and Analysis of ROZ20
The extract of ginger described herein was prepared and then analyzed to
determine the identity of the major components. This analysis was done by
HPLC (high pressure liquid chromatography). The extract of ginger was then
mixed with dried, powdered ginger to form the ROZ20 composition of the
present invention. The preparative and analytical methods were as follows.
First, the ginger extract of the present invention was prepared from the
ginger raw material, ginger rhizomes, as follows. Approximately 250 kg of
ginger raw material was milled with a mill screen of 10 mm. The first
extraction was performed by adding a minimum of 1000 liters of ethanol 90%
(VYV) to the ginger raw material, which was then allowed to stand at 50 °C for
1 hour. The extract was then separated from the remaining particulate material

by filtration.
At this point, the first extract could have been evaporated, substantially
as descπbed below, to form an oleoresin extract, which could also have been
microencapsulated, substantially as described below. However, preferably the
second extraction was performed on the remaining particulate material with a
similar volume of ethanol, but the mixture was only allowed to stand for one
half of an hour. A third extraction was also preferably performed. The third
extraction was similar to the second extraction, except that only a minimum of
750 liters of ethanol 90% (VYV) was added.
The extracts were preferably combined and then were concentrated
under a vacuum pressure of 500 mm Hg with gradual heating to a maximum
temperature of 60 °C until a minimum of 90% TDS (Total Dissolved
Substances) has been reached. The extract was then concentrated further by
evaporation at a temperature which does not exceed 60 °C. The evaporation
continued for one additional hour until no more liquid was visible, thereby
forming a dried combined extract. At this point, the extract was at least 95%
TDS and was then cooled to room temperature.
After cooling, the extract was analyzed for gingerols and shogaols
substantially as described below. The ginger extract was then combined by
being microencapsulated with dried, powdered ginger rhizome which
contained known concentrations of gingerols and shogaols to form the ROZ20
composition of the present invention. The weight percent ratio of the amount
of extract to the amount of powdered rhizome was in a range of a ratio of from

about 1 to about 9, to a ratio of from about 2 to about 8. The
microencapsulation was performed by spheronizing ginger extract and
powdered rhizome with a binder, preferably a water soluble cellulose
derivative, to form small spheres,, preferably of about 1000 microns diameter.
The spheres were then preferably further coated with a cellulose derivative. In
the prefeπed embodiment, the complete ROZ20 extract was a combination of
from about 90 percent to about 95 percent material derived from ginger and
from about 5 percent to about 10 percent cellulose derivatives, weight per
weight.
The HPLC (high pressure liquid chromatography) analysis was
performed substantially as described in the Seventh Supplement, USP - NF ,
Official Monographs, NF 18 page 4095 (United States Pharmacopeial
Convention Inc., Rockville, Maryland, USA). Briefly, the mobile phase
featured acetonitrile, dilute phosphoric acid (1 in 1000) and methanol (55:44: 1).
The column was a 4.6 mm x 25 cm Lichrocart column, RP - 18 endcapped,
which was packed with LI (Lichrospher 100 (5 microns); catalog number
50838, Merck, USA). The flow rate was 1 ml/min.
As a standard for quantification, a standard solution of 0.25 mg per
milliter of USP capsaicin RS was prepared. Fifty milligrams of the ginger
extract of the present invention was then dissolved in 10 milliliters of methanol
to form a ginger extract solution. Ten microliters of the standard solution
and ten microliters of the ginger extract solution were then separately injected

into the HPLC after preparation of the column.
Figure 2B shows the results of the HPLC analysis. As shown, peak
number 2 is 6-gingerol and peak number 4 is 6-shogaol, both of which are
clearly the major components of the gmger extract and hence of the ROZ20
composition of the present invention. In addition, a peak for 8-gingerol is
seen at 13.81 minutes, a peak for 6-gιngerodiol at 23.83 minutes, a peak for
10-gingerol at 30.65 minutes and a peak for 8-shogaol at 37.63 minutes.
However, it should be noted that other peaks are also present, and are
not necessarily excluded as being one or more of the active component or
components of ROZ20 responsible for the effects of the ROZ20 composition of
the present invention (see Example 2 for a descπption of the effects). These
other peaks are believed also to be potentially effective as a treatment for
atherosclerosis and as such lie within the scope of the present Application.
In particular, ginger rhizome has been shown to contain gingerols and
shogaols, as shown in Figure 2A. Both gingerols and shogaols are families of
structurally related compounds as shown. Ginger rhizome contains 6-, 8- and
10-gingerol and -shogaol. As described previously for Figure 3, all of these
compounds are clearly contained within the ROZ20 extract of the present
invention. Thus, all of these compounds may be described as a "component
of ginger" and therefore lie within the scope of the present invention.
Furthermore, since the ROZ20 composition of the present invention is
a mixture of both the ginger extract, prepared as described above, and dried,
powdered ginger, dried ginger rhizome also contains one or more components

of ginger and as such also lies within the scope of the present invention.
Example 2
Testing the Effect of ROZ20 on
Atherosclerosis in E~ Mice
The effect of the composition of the present invention, ROZ20, on the
pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in E (apolipoprotein E-deficient) mice was
tested. Briefly, the mice were fed ROZ20 in the diet for varying lengths of
time. The mice were then sacrificed and various parameters of atherosclerosis
were analyzed, including the visual inspection of the arteries for the formation
of atherosclerotic plaques. ROZ20 was shown to be highly effective for
preventing the formation of atherosclerotic plaques in these mice. The
experimental method was as follows.
METHODS
Sixty apolipoprotein E deficient (E ) mice, 6 weeks of age, were divided
into 3 groups, with 20 mice in each group. The study was performed in two
consecutive experiments, each experiment using 60 mice. The mice received a
dietary supplement in their drinking water which was selected from one of the
following:
a) placebo (control group);
b) 25 μg/day/mouse of ROZ20; or
c) 250 μg/day/mouse of ROZ20.
LDL was isolated from blood samples drawn from the E mice before

administration of the composition, and at two and ten weeks after
administration, by discontinuous density gradient ultracentrifugation (48). The
resultant fraction was dialyzed against saline with EDTA ( 1 mmol/L). Before
the oxidation study was performed, the fraction containing LDL was diluted in
phosphate buffered saline (PBS) to 200 mg protein/L and dialyzed overnight
against PBS at 4 °C to remove EDTA. LDL protein concentration in the
fraction was determined with the Folin phenol reagent (49).
LDL oxidation and aggregation
Oxidation of LDL was carried out in a shaking water bath at 37 C under
air, in plastic tubes, 1 cm in diameter. For metal ion-dependent oxidation, LDL
was incubated for 4h at 37 °C with freshly prepared CuS04 (5μmol/L).
Oxidation was terminated by refrigeration at 4 °C and by the addition of
0.1 mmol/L EDTA to chelate the copper ions. LDL oxidation was determined
by measuring the amount of thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS)
Formation of conjugated dienes was continuously monitored by
measuring the increase in absorbance at 234 nm (51 ). Incubations were carried
out in the spectrophotometer cuvette at 37 °C in a temperature-controlled six
cell holder in a spectrophotometer (Ultrospec 3000, Pharmacia, Biotech). The
reference cell contained 5 μmol/L CuS04 in PBS, or 1 mmol/L of AAPH
together with 0.1 mM EDTA in PBS, for the examination of metal ion
dependent or metal ion-independent oxidation, respectively. The initial

background of the different samples ranged between 0.1-0.2 O.D. as recorded
at 234nm. However, after recording the initial absorbance, the
spectrophotometer was set to zero against the blank, and the increase in
absorbance occurring during LDL oxidation was recorded over time every ten
minutes.
The extent of LDL associated lipid peroxide formation was determined
with a commercially available kit (cholesterol color reagent, CHOD iodide
method, Diagnostica Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) (52). This assay is based on
the oxidative activity of lipid peroxides which convert iodide to iodine, and
which can be measured spectrophotometrically. The assay was performed with
100 μl of lipoprotein solution ( 100 mg protein/ml) which was mixed on a
vortex with 1 ml of color reagent from the manufacturer. The sample was
allowed to stand for 30 minutes in the dark followed by the measurement of
absorbance at 365 nm against a blank.
LDL aggregation was induced by vigorous vortexing of the sample. The
optical density at 680 nm was measured every 10 seconds. Increased optical
density of the sample indicated the presence of LDL aggregation.
Mouse peritoneal macrophage preparation
Mouse peritoneal macrophages (MPM) were harvested from the
peritoneal fluid of the E mice (15-25g) 4 days after intraperitoneal injection
into each mouse of 3ml of thioglycolate (24g/l) in saline. The cells (10-20 x
10 cells per mouse) were washed and centrifuged three times with phosphate-

buffered saline (PBS) at lOOOg for 10 min, then re-suspended in DMEM
containing 15% horse serum (heat-inactivated at 56° C for 30min), 100 U/ml
penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, and 2 mM glutamine for a final
concentration of 10 cells per liter. The cell suspension was dispensed into 35
mm plastic Petri dishes and incubated in a humidified incubator (5% C02, 95%
air) for 2 hours. The dishes were washed once with 5 ml DMEM to remove
nonadherent cells, and the monolayer was then incubated under similar
conditions for 18 hours prior to the beginning of the experiment.
LDL oxidation bv macrophages
Cells (10 cells per 35 mm dish) were incubated in the incubator with the
fraction containing LDL (0.2 mg protein/ml) in DMEM supplemented with 1

Histopathology of aortic atherosclerotic lesion
The histopathological analysis of the lesions was performed as follows.
At the end of the experimental period the mice were anesthetized with ethyl
ether in a local nasal container. The heart and entire aorta were rapidly
dissected out and immersion fixed in 3% glutaraldehyde in 0.1M sodium
cacodylate buffer with 0.0 1% calcium chloride, pH 7.4 at room temperature.
After approximately one hour, under a binocular stereomicroscope, the aortic
arch was dissected free from the surrounding fatty tissue and the first four
millimeters of the ascending aorta (beginning with the aortic valves) was
removed and cut transversely with razor blades into four blocks of approx. 1
mm each. The samples were kept in the fixative at room temperature
overnight. The samples were then rinsed and stored in 0.1M sodium cacodylate
buffer containing 7.5% w/v sucrose prior to treatment with an unbuffered 1%
aqueous solution of osmium tetroxide for 4 hours. This was followed by
cacodylate rinse and dehydration in ascending ethanols, prior to propylene
oxide and embedding in epoxy resin ("Eponate 12", Pelco Int., Redding, CA).
The blocks were orientated so that the transverse section of the aorta
could be cut. After heat polymerization for 18 hours at 60 °C, the blocks were
trimmed and one micron sections were cut with glass or diamond knives on an
LKB "Nova" ultramicrotome (LKB, Bromma, Sweden). The sections were
mounted on glass slides and stained with 0. 1% toluidine blue in 1% borax
(sodium tetraborate). In these toluidine blue stained sections, the lipid deposits

appear to have a green color and are easily visualized. When sufficient semi-
thin sections were sampled from all the blocks, the remainder of the blocks
were then cut into much thicker sections ( 150-200μm) for more macroscopic
observation. The lipid content of the lesions of these thicker sections was
stained an intense black from the prolonged osmium treatment, so that the
delineation of the areas of atherosclerotic lesions was easily determined
histomorphometrically. (The thinner toluidine blue sections, as seen in the
micrographs, permitted observations on the histopathological development of
the lesions at a higher resolution and also allowed further cutting for
transmission electron microscopy). Only the area of the aortic arch was
examined as previous studies have shown that this area is especially prone to
atherosclerosis in the Apolipoprotein E-deficient mice.

VLDL and VLDL-remnant are the main lipid earners in the

LDL derived from control mice receiving placebo for 2 weeks was
minimally oxidized, as shown by 4.9 Nome MDA/mg protein (Figure 3A) and

time needed for oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids within the VLDL,

the ROZ20 composition of the present invention, a lag time of 80 minutes was

deficient mice with ROZ20 was shown to reduce the basal oxidative state and

Since VLDL is the main lipid carrier lipoprotein in E° mice, and ROZ20

of the present invention markedly affected VLDL oxidation following 2 weeks

invention on the capacity of peritoneal macrophages to oxidativelv modify
LDL.
Cells of the arterial well, including macrophages, are known to oxidize
LDL in vivo. The ability of the cells to oxidize the lipoprotein is the result of
the balance between cellular oxidants and antioxidants. Consumption of
ROZ20 resulted in reduced susceptibility of isolated LDL and VLDL to

oxidation. However, when ingested, antioxidant components in the ROZ20
composition of the present invention may become incorporated into cells, thus
affecting their oxidative status. Thus, after 10 weeks of treatment with ROZ20,
peritoneal macrophages were harvested from E mice which consumed placebo,
25μg/day ROZ20, or 250μg/day ROZ20. The cells were then incubated with
lOOμg of protein of human LDL/ml under conditions of oxidative stress
generated by adding 5μM CUS04 to the incubation medium. LDL incubated
under similar conditions but without cells served as a control. Figure 19A
shows that when LDL was incubated with peritoneal macrophages (MPM)
derived from mice which consumed 25 μg/day or 250μg/day ROZ20,
respectively, as compared to LDL incubated with MPM from the placebo

respectively, was obtained from the TBARS assay. Furthermore, a reduction in

treatment with ROZ20 may also affect cells in the arterial wall by reducing
their capacity to oxidatively modify native LDL. Since strong evidence
suggests that the oxidation of LDL in vivo occurs in extracellular spaces in the
arterial wall, and is probably mediated by cells of the arterial wall, reduction in
the oxidative capacity of the cells by oral administration of ROZ20 may
represent an important intervention to reduce the rate of development of

atherosclerosis.
VII. The effect of ROZ20 consumption on cholesterol metabolism in
macrophages
Cholesterol is an essential component of all animal cell membranes.
Excess accumulation of cholesterol in cells is avoided by maintaining a balance
between external sources via the receptor-mediated endocytosis of lipoproteins,
and the internal sources from de novo cellular synthesis. Cellular uptake of
LDL is mediated via the LDL receptor, whose activity is regulated by the
cellular cholesterol level. However, as was mentioned before, oxidative
modification of LDL leads to its recognition and endocytosis via the scavenger
receptors, which are not subjected to cellular cholesterol regulation. This
process therefore can lead to cholesterol accumulation in the cells and to foam
cell formation. Therefore, the effect of treatment with ROZ20 on the
cholesterol metabolism in macrophages was examined.
First, the effect of treatment with ROZ20 on the cellular cholesterol
synthesis rate was examined. As shown in Figure 20, demonstrates
macrophages derived from mice which consumed 25μg/day or 250μg/day of
ginger extract for 10 weeks were shown to have a reduction of 36% or 16% in
the rate of cellular cholesterol synthesis, respectively. Next, the effect of
ROZ20 consumption on the cellular uptake of LDL and of oxidized - LDL (Ox-
LDL) was examined. Figure 21 demonstrates that the incubation of radio-
iodinated LDL with macrophages derived from mice which consumed
25μg/day or 250μg/day of ROZ20 resulted in decreased cellular degradation of

LDL of 66% or 61%, respectively (Figure 21 A), and decreased cellular
association of the LDL of 65% and 59%, respectively (Figure 2 IB), in
compaπson to cellular degradation and cell association of LDL by macrophages
derived from control mice.
Although the Ox-LDL receptor is not regulated by the cellular
cholesterol level, a 50% inhibition in cellular deactivation (Figure 22A) and
cellular association (Figure 22B) of OX-LDL was found in macrophages from
mice treated with ROZ20, in comparison to Ox-LDL uptake by macrophages
from mice given the placebo. Thus, treatment with ROZ20 appears to affect
cellular lipoprotein uptake, probably by mechanisms independent of the cellular
cholesterol level.

after treatment with the ROZ20 composition of the present invention
At the end of 10 weeks of consumption of 250μg/day ROZ20, the mice
were sacrificed and the entire aorta was rapidly dissected as described in
"Methods". Aortic arches obtained from all mice studied (control and those
treated with ROZ20) showed atherosclerotic lesions. However, in all cases the
lesion areas in the aortic arches of ROZ20 treated mice were considerably
smaller than the lesions in the arches of mice treated with placebo (Figure 23).

for a period of 10 weeks to the atherosclerotic E mice has a significant
beneficial effect in substantially reducing the size and rate of development of
atherosclerotic lesions.

1. A composition for treating an atherosclerotic condition, comprising
a component selected from the group consisting of 6-shogaol, 8-shogaol, 10-
shogaol, 6-gingerol, 8-gingerol and 10-gingerol, and a mixture thereof.
2. The composition of claim 1 , wherein said component is selected
from the group consisting of 6-shogaol and 6-gingerol.
3. The composition of claim 2, wherein said component is 6-shogaol.
4. The composition of claim 2, wherein said component is 6-gingerol.
5. The composition of claim 1 , further comprising a dried ginger
extract.
6. The composition of claim 5, further comprising powdered rhizome.
7. The composition of claim 6, wherein said dried ginger extract is
microencapsulated with said powdered rhizome.
8. A composition for treating an atherosclerotic condition, comprising
a dried gmger extract.
9. The composition of claim 8, further compπsing powdered rhizome.
10. The composition of claim 9, wherein said dried ginger extract is
microencapsulated with said powdered rhizome.

ROZ20.
12. A method for the treatment of an atherosclerotic condition in a
subject, comprising the step of administering a pharmaceutically effective
amount of a component selected from the group consisting of a 6-shogaol, 8-
shogaol, 10-shogaol, 6-gingerol, 8-gingerol and 10-gingerol, and a mixture
thereof; dried ginger rhizome alone or in combination with one of the
aforementioned ingredients; and ROZ20, alone or in combination with one of the
aforementioned ingredients.
13. The method of claim 12, wherein said component includes ROZ20.
14. The method of claim 12, wherein said component is selected from
the group consisting of a 6-shogaol, 8-shogaol, 10-shogaol, 6-gingerol, 8-
gingerol and 10-gingerol, and a mixture thereof.
15. The method of claim 14, wherein said component includes dried
ginger rhizome.
16. A method for preparation of a ginger extract, the method comprising
the steps of:
(a) extracting ginger rhizome with a first volume of an ethanol solvent
to form a first extract and a first residue;
(b) separating said first extract and said first residue;
(c) evaporating said first extract to form an oleoresin extract; and
(d) mixing said oleoresin extract with dried, powdered ginger rhizome
to form the ginger extract.
17. The method of claim 16, wherein the step of mixing said oleoresin
extract with said dried, powdered ginger rhizome is performed by
microencapsulating said oleoresin extract and said dried, powdered ginger
rhizome.
18. The method of claim 16, wherein said ethanol solvent is 90% (VYV)
ethanol.

19. The method of claim 16, further comprising the steps of:
(e) extracting said first residue with a second volume of said ethanol
solvent to form a second extract and a second residue;
(f) separating said second extract and said second residue;
(g) extracting said second residue with a third volume of said ethanol to
form a third extract and a third residue;
(h) separating said third extract and said third residue;
(i) combining said first extract, said second extract and said third
extract to form a combined extract;
(j) evaporating said combined extract to form a combined dried extract;
and
(k) mixing said combined dried extract with said dried, powdered ginger
rhizome to form the ginger extract.
20. The method of claim 19, wherein said ginger rhizome is milled

composition prepared according to the method of claim 19.
